take.title: Take one back to your team
take.description: Nothing here is graded or checked. 4 of the 5 points are things to work out rather than build; the tick is purely a bookmark.
take.queue.label: Write down what still stands between your finished work and production, and cross off everything that is just typing.
take.sentence.label: Write down the sentence you are going to say at the next demo about what the rough version does not do yet.
take.line.label: Pick 1 correction you gave an agent more than 1 time this week, and write it into the repository's own CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md.
take.practice.label: Pick 1 ritual your team holds on to, write down which constraint it was once invented for, and say whether that constraint is still there.
take.person.label: Put one of the first 4 points to 1 person on your team. Write down a name and a date.
pipeline-shift.description: The same 5 stages 2 times, drawn on one scale. Above, the way it ran when a person typed the code: deciding, waiting, a wide block of writing, verifying, releasing. Below, the way it runs with agents: writing is a sliver run as 3 lanes at once, verifying is the widest solid block, and both waiting stages are wider than they were. Under that second row, a dashed strip shows the verifying 3 lanes need. It runs well past the block above it, and a mark on it shows where the checking actually stopped.
pipeline-shift.caption: The times are illustrative. The scale is not: both rows are drawn against one clock, and the strip under the second is 3 lanes of output at what 1 lane cost to read.
sdlc-stages.today.name: Today
sdlc-stages.today.body: 6 departments and 5 handovers. The build phase takes the most time and therefore sets the pace of the whole process.
sdlc-stages.assisted.name: AI-assisted
sdlc-stages.assisted.body: Agents build. The bottleneck moves to what you asked for and to whoever checks it.
sdlc-stages.native.name: The AI-native chain
sdlc-stages.native.body: With handovers a thing of the past, the work runs in one smooth flow. Only 4 human decision points still set the final speed.
sdlc-stages.return: What happens in production feeds the next piece of work
sdlc-stages.legend.waits: Where the run narrows, the work waits
sdlc-stages.caption: After the AI-native SDLC on smartagents.be, which builds on Anthropic's AI-native SDLC playbook.
quiz.three-weeks-after-thursday.question: On Thursday you demo a working feature and everyone considers it 'done'. 3 weeks later, however, you are still coding on it, with nothing waiting on a review or a release window. Where did those 3 weeks go?
quiz.three-weeks-after-thursday.cases: To unforeseen situations; edge cases nobody had in mind while writing the request, or that only arose when the feature was already half done.
quiz.three-weeks-after-thursday.vague: The scope was too vague; with a sharper request these edge cases would already have surfaced in the first run.
quiz.three-weeks-after-thursday.poor: The agent's implementation was of low quality, so almost everything had to be redone by hand.
quiz.three-weeks-after-thursday.queue: To automated testing; the demo ran on untested code that still needed tests.
quiz.three-weeks-after-thursday.explanat: An agent implements the request it was given, along the path you described. A sharper first draft does not produce the detail nobody knew about yet, so the burden moved rather than lifted.
quiz.their-prototype.question: During lunch, a manager put together a working prototype and shows it in the meeting. The code has no validation and uses a hard-coded user. What do you do?
quiz.their-prototype.say: You name what is still missing right away, out loud, in the meeting.
quiz.their-prototype.theirs: You say nothing; it is their prototype, so it is up to them to point out the caveats.
quiz.their-prototype.ticket: You record the missing parts in a ticket, so the decision makers can read them.
quiz.their-prototype.build: You first build a full version and then show what a finished product looks like.
quiz.their-prototype.explanation: What it does not do gets said either way. Left out now, it is said later by somebody asking why the feature they signed off on falls over on an empty list.
quiz.one-afternoon-quarter.question: Work that used to take a week was now done in a single afternoon. Your manager asks what output the team can commit to this quarter. What do you answer?
quiz.one-afternoon-quarter.checkpoint: The next checkpoint and what will be done by then; after all, that 1 afternoon is only 1 data point.
quiz.one-afternoon-quarter.fourtimes: 4 times the old output; after all, that afternoon shows the new pace.
quiz.one-afternoon-quarter.old: The original estimate; after all, 1 fast run says nothing about a whole quarter.
quiz.one-afternoon-quarter.average: The average of the last 3 runs; you will not get a more accurate indication of speed.
quiz.one-afternoon-quarter.explanation: Hand the same request over 2 times and it does not come back the same 2 times. 1 afternoon is a single reading of a job that has changed shape, too few to set a new rate on.
deck.change.test-engineer.title: You are <hi>the test engineer</hi> now
deck.change.test-engineer.note: Reading every line stops scaling. The case the agent did not think of does.
deck.change.business.title: Knowing the domain is <hi>not scope creep</hi>
deck.change.business.note: A version by Thursday only helps if somebody who knows what it was for looks at it on Thursday.
deck.change.pipelines.title: The process was <hi>the bottleneck</hi>
deck.change.decides.title: A person still decides <hi>4 times</hi>
deck.change.rethink.title: The way of working is <hi>a decision</hi>
deck.change.rethink.2: Review, when <mute>an agent wrote the diff</mute>
deck.change.gates.title: Taste relaxes. <hi>The gates do not.</hi>
deck.change.environment.title: The deliverable is <hi>the environment</hi>, <mute>not this quarter</mute>
deck.change.environment.note: Count the times this week you told an agent something you had told it before. Each one is a line missing from a file.
deck.expectations.floor.title: Productivity gains from AI are available to everyone: they are <hi>the new floor</hi>, <mute>not a unique advantage</mute>
deck.expectations.missing.title: Take charge of <hi>what is still missing</hi>
deck.expectations.missing.1: <hi>Name the gap straight away:</hi> Say of your own accord what is still missing as soon as you show a first version or prototype.
deck.expectations.missing.2: <hi>The inevitable feedback:</hi> That remark is coming anyway; the only question is whether you take charge, or someone else has to ask about it afterwards.
deck.expectations.missing.3: <hi>A stronger position:</hi> By putting the missing parts on the table right away, you steer the conversation towards the content instead of towards defending yourself.
deck.expectations.burden.title: The illusion of <hi>'done on Thursday'</hi>
deck.expectations.burden.1: <hi>The 80/20 trap:</hi> A quick prototype version is only the beginning.
deck.expectations.burden.2: <hi>Unforeseen complexity:</hi> 3 weeks of polishing exceptions nobody could have written down beforehand.
deck.expectations.burden.3: <hi>The lesson:</hi> Only count it as 'done' once the edge cases are handled robustly.
deck.expectations.estimate.title: Human review sets <hi>the delivery date</hi>
deck.expectations.estimate.1: <hi>Honest planning:</hi> Always name a delivery date that explicitly includes the time for thorough review.
deck.expectations.estimate.2: <hi>The human bottleneck:</hi> Agents generate code much faster, but your reading speed and capacity to take it in stay the same.
deck.expectations.estimate.3: <hi>1 definition of 'done':</hi> Avoid miscommunication at the table: 'done generating' is something very different from 'ready for production'.
deck.expectations.velocity.title: From occasional outliers to <hi>predictable steering</hi>
deck.expectations.velocity.1: <hi>Outlier vs. velocity:</hi> 1 flawless run is a single sample, not a structural development speed (velocity).
deck.expectations.velocity.2: <hi>Milestones over promises:</hi> Promise stakeholders the next measurable checkpoint, not the finish line straight away.
deck.expectations.velocity.3: <hi>Predictable steering:</hi> By reporting step by step you stay in charge and avoid disappointment when an unforeseen delay comes.
deck.impostor.engineer.title: You are still <hi>the engineer</hi>
deck.impostor.engineer.1: <hi>Autonomous execution:</hi> The agent decides the route: how the code is built up and which steps are taken.
deck.impostor.engineer.2: <hi>Human direction:</hi> You set the goal, secure the verification and supply the judgement.
deck.impostor.engineer.3: <hi>Final responsibility:</hi> The machine generates, but you remain the architect who vouches for the quality.
deck.impostor.signal.title: Tell the feeling from <hi>the signal</hi>
deck.impostor.signal.note: Do not let a 'working diff' blind you.
deck.impostor.signal.1: <hi>Feeling vs. signal:</hi> A diff you cannot follow is a signal; doubting yourself after following every line is often just a feeling.
deck.impostor.signal.2: <hi>The diff trap:</hi> A code change (diff) you cannot follow yourself is not a solved problem: it is a gap in your knowledge filled with generated code.
deck.impostor.signal.3: <hi>Critical checking:</hi> Keep understanding the steps taken before you approve, or you lose control of the codebase.
deck.impostor.written.title: Nobody has been doing this <hi>long</hi>
deck.impostor.written.note: The tools evolved 2 times already while this course was being written. The only trace? A file that stopped needing the same correction.
deck.change.divider.1: <hi>Value over code:</hi> Producing code was never the real goal; delivering the right business value is.
deck.change.divider.2: <hi>Continuous alignment:</hi> Involve the business in the process every week, instead of a one-off reveal at the demo.
deck.change.divider.3: <hi>The real delay:</hi> Typing code by hand was never the real bottleneck in the planning calendar.
deck.expectations.divider.1: <hi>The first-impression trap:</hi> Demonstrating 1 fast afternoon creates the illusion that everything can be done in an afternoon from now on.
deck.expectations.divider.2: <hi>Review is part of the estimate:</hi> A realistic time estimate always includes thoroughly checking, testing and verifying the output.
deck.expectations.divider.3: <hi>A shift in effort:</hi> The total workload has not gone away, it has moved from typing by hand to critical checking.
deck.impostor.divider.1: <hi>The danger of ease:</hi> The impostor feeling strikes precisely when the agent performs well.
deck.impostor.divider.2: Good judgement produces no extra lines of code by 5 p.m., but it does give you control.
deck.impostor.divider.3: Only what you explicitly document and automate builds lasting value.
